You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

text
π method mean ζ κ coverage of complete-data ζ_full still detected 0.20 Listwise 0.434 0.062 0.999 0.44 0.20 MI-pooled 0.266 0.425 0.967 0.06 0.20 MI-group-wise 0.425 0.081 0.996 0.40 0.40 Listwise 0.399 0.136 0.986 0.24 0.40 MI-pooled 0.069 0.850 0.741 0.00 0.40 MI-group-wise 0.389 0.160 0.985 0.22 With 40% of sepal-width values missing, the default imputation model returns ζ = 0.07 against a complete-data 0.46 and detects the species difference in none of 2000 replications. Group-wise imputation detects it as often as listwise deletion does. The pooled model does not merely cost power; it removes the effect. 5a. The real data transports the theory to a design it was not derived for This is a worked application on one familiar dataset, repeatedly masked -a transport check, not replication across datasets or data-generating processes. The population the quadrature evaluates is a bivariate normal fitted to iris, so every “exact” figure below is exact in that fitted population and not in the finite, non-normal sample.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 895 columns across 78 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 78 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

  • assemble_paper3.py calls os.chdir(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 38 statistical tests reported in the paper, 22 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 83 R code files.

File paths

5 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: simulation_functions.R to R/simulation_functions.R (in aggregate_from_raw.R); disagrees with results/quadratic_kappa_curve.csv to results/quadratic_kappa_curve.csv (in fig_moment_defect_structure.R); simulation_functions.R to R/simulation_functions.R (in make_intuition_figures.R); simulation_functions.R to R/simulation_functions.R (in run_mi_variants.R); simulation_functions.R to R/simulation_functions.R (in run_simulation.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 10 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged. 86 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 83 scripts: 61 ran without error, 11 errored, 5 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 6 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it, so before running it once more we copied it there: p36imp_osf_bundle_20261007_v5.zip/osf_bundle/results/sequel_grid.csv to p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/results/sequel_grid.csv for p36imp_osf_bundle_paper1_2026-10-27_2044_56f9ba37.zip/osf_bundle/scripts/check_numbers.R. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

> set.seed(4004)
> zeta_plim <- function(rho1, rho2, pi_t, gy = 0.7, nref = 4e6) {
>   # selection moments from a large reference draw of Y ~ N(0,1)
>   y  <- rnorm(nref)
>   g0 <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + gy * y)) - pi_t, c(-30, 30))$root
>   R  <- runif(nref) >= plogis(g0 + gy * y)          # TRUE = observed
>   p_o <- mean(R); p_m <- 1 - p_o
>   m1_o <- mean(y[R]);  m2_o <- mean(y[R]^2)
>   m1_m <- mean(y[!R]); m2_m <- mean(y[!R]^2)
>   v_o  <- m2_o - m1_o^2
>   A <- p_o * m2_o; B <- p_m * m2_m
> 
>   b   <- (rho1 + rho2) / 2                          # pooled slope
>   rr  <- c(rho1, rho2)
>   s2  <- mean(rr^2 * v_o + 1 - rr^2) - b^2 * v_o    # pooled residual variance
> 
>   r_g <- vapply(rr, function(rho) {
>     k    <- (rho - b) * m1_o
>     cov  <- rho * A + b * B + k * p_m * m1_m
>     ex   <- p_o * rho * m1_o + p_m * (k + b * m1_m)
>     ex2  <- p_o * (rho^2 * m2_o + 1 - rho^2) +
>             p_m * (k^2 + 2 * k * b * m1_m + b^2 * m2_m + s2)
>     cov / sqrt(ex2 - ex^2)
>   }, numeric(1))
>   atanh(r_g[1]) - atanh(r_g[2])
> }
> zeta_sim <- function(rho1, rho2, pi_t, gy = 0.7, N = 4e6) {
>   n1 <- N / 2
>   G  <- rep(1:2, each = n1)
>   rho <- ifelse(G == 1, rho1, rho2)
>   y  <- rnorm(N)
>   x  <- rho * y + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N)
>   g0 <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + gy * y)) - pi_t, c(-30, 30))$root
>   mis <- runif(N) < plogis(g0 + gy * y)
>   fit <- lm(x[!mis] ~ y[!mis] + factor(G[!mis]))    # POOLED slope, group main effect
>   cf  <- coef(fit); s <- sigma(fit)
>   xs  <- x
>   km  <- cf[1] + ifelse(G[mis] == 2, cf[3], 0)
>   xs[mis] <- km + cf[2] * y[mis] + s * rnorm(sum(mis))
>   r1 <- cor(xs[G == 1], y[G == 1]); r2 <- cor(xs[G == 2], y[G == 2])
>   atanh(r1) - atanh(r2)
> }
> designs <- list(

>   s2 <- sum(c(a, 1 - a) * ((beta_g - b)^2 * v + tau2_g))

>     var <- v[g] * b^2 + s2 + f * (v[g] * (beta_g[g]^2 - b^2) + tau2_g[g] - s2)
>     cov / sqrt(v[g] * var)
>   })
> }

> GZY <- 0.7
> ols <- function(y, X) {                    # coefficients + residual variance
>   b <- solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))
>   r <- y - X %*% b
>   list(b = as.numeric(b), s2 = sum(r^2) / length(y))
> }
> run_one <- function(b3, observed_only, seed = 20261002L) {
>   set.seed(seed)
>   z1 <- rnorm(N); z2 <- rnorm(N)
>   X1 <- z1; X2 <- RHO * z1 + sqrt(1 - RHO^2) * z2
>   Y  <- B1 * X1 + B2 * X2 + b3 * X1 * X2 + rnorm(N, 0, SIG)
> 
>   # The mechanism, z-scored on this sample's own moments and calibrated
>   # so the expected missing rate is RATE -- as calibrate_mar() does.
>   eta <- GZ2 * (X2 - mean(X2)) / sd(X2) + GZY * (Y - mean(Y)) / sd(Y)
>   g0  <- uniroot(function(g) mean(plogis(g + eta)) - RATE, c(-20, 20),
>                  tol = 1e-12)$root
>   mis <- runif(N) < plogis(g0 + eta)
>   obs <- !mis
> 
>   # Initialize exactly as impute_smc_draw() does.
>   x1 <- X1; x1[mis] <- NA
>   init <- ols(X1[obs], cbind(1, X2[obs], Y[obs]))$b
>   x1[mis] <- init[1] + init[2] * X2[mis] + init[3] * Y[mis]
> 
>   trace <- matrix(NA_real_, ITERS, 2,
>                   dimnames = list(NULL, c("cov_slope", "interaction")))
>   for (it in seq_len(ITERS)) {
>     o  <- ols(Y, cbind(1, x1, X2, x1 * X2))
>     a  <- o$b; s2 <- o$s2
>     if (observed_only) {
>       c_ <- ols(X1[obs], cbind(1, X2[obs]))        # the defect
>     } else {
>       c_ <- ols(x1, cbind(1, X2))                  # eq. (6): completed vector
>     }
>     d0 <- c_$b[1]; d1 <- c_$b[2]; tau2 <- c_$s2
> 
>     a_i  <- a[2] + a[4] * X2[mis]
>     c_i  <- a[1] + a[3] * X2[mis]
>     prec <- 1 / tau2 + a_i^2 / s2
>     mu   <- ((d0 + d1 * X2[mis]) / tau2 + a_i * (Y[mis] - c_i) / s2) / prec
>     x1[mis] <- rnorm(sum(mis), mu, sqrt(1 / prec))
>     trace[it, ] <- c(d1, a[4])
>   }
>   trace

>   V  <- chol2inv(qr.R(qrZ))                            # (Z'Z)^-1

> .gmom <- function(mu, sd, a, gy, k, missing) {
>   f <- function(y) {
>     w <- plogis(a + gy * y)
>     y^k * dnorm(y, mu, sd) * (if (missing) w else 1 - w)
>   }
>   integrate(f, mu - 12 * sd, mu + 12 * sd, rel.tol = 1e-11,
>             subdivisions = 500L)$value
> }
> applied_plim <- function(groups, pi_t, gy = 0.7, share = c(0.5, 0.5)) {
>   # calibrate the intercept so the OVERALL missing fraction equals pi_t
>   overall_missing <- function(a)
>     sum(vapply(seq_along(groups), function(g)
>       share[g] * .gmom(groups[[g]]$muY, groups[[g]]$sdY, a, gy, 0, TRUE),
>       numeric(1)))
>   a <- uniroot(function(a) overall_missing(a) - pi_t, c(-40, 40),
>                tol = 1e-12)$root
> 
>   G <- length(groups)
>   st <- vector("list", G)
>   for (g in seq_len(G)) {
>     p <- groups[[g]]
>     beta <- p$rho * p$sdX / p$sdY
>     resv <- p$sdX^2 * (1 - p$rho^2)
> 
>     p_o <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 0, FALSE)      # P(observed) within group
>     p_m <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 0, TRUE)
>     EYo  <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 1, FALSE) / p_o
>     EY2o <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 2, FALSE) / p_o
>     EYm  <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 1, TRUE)  / p_m
>     EY2m <- .gmom(p$muY, p$sdY, a, gy, 2, TRUE)  / p_m
>     VYo  <- EY2o - EYo^2
> 
>     EXo   <- p$muX + beta * (EYo - p$muY)            # X | Y linear, so this is exact
>     CovXY <- beta * VYo
>     VXo   <- beta^2 * VYo + resv
> 
>     st[[g]] <- list(p_o = p_o, p_m = p_m, EYo = EYo, EY2o = EY2o,
>                     EYm = EYm, EY2m = EY2m, VYo = VYo, EXo = EXo,
>                     CovXY = CovXY, VXo = VXo, beta = beta, resv = resv,
>                     muY = p$muY, sdY = p$sdY, muX = p$muX, rho = p$rho)
>   }
> 
>   # observed-sample composition -- this is what makes b asymmetric
>   wt <- vapply(seq_len(G), function(g) share[g] * st[[g]]$p_o, numeric(1))
>   q  <- wt / sum(wt)
> 
>   b <- sum(q * vapply(st, `[[`, numeric(1), "CovXY")) /
>        sum(q * vapply(st, `[[`, numeric(1), "VYo"))
>   s2 <- sum(q * vapply(st, function(z)
>     z$VXo - 2 * b * z$CovXY + b^2 * z$VYo, numeric(1)))
> 
>   r_pool <- r_group <- numeric(G)
>   for (g in seq_len(G)) {
>     z <- st[[g]]
>     f <- z$p_o / (z$p_o + z$p_m)                     # fraction observed in group
>     alpha <- z$EXo - b * z$EYo                       # group intercept, pooled fit
> 
>     # ---- pooled imputation ------------------------------------------------
>     EXs  <- f * z$EXo + (1 - f) * (alpha + b * z$EYm)
>     EX2s <- f * (z$VXo + z$EXo^2) +
>             (1 - f) * (alpha^2 + 2 * alpha * b * z$EYm + b^2 * z$EY2m + s2)
>     EXYs <- f * (z$CovXY + z$EXo * z$EYo) +
>             (1 - f) * (alpha * z$EYm + b * z$EY2m)
>     EY  <- z$muY; EY2 <- z$sdY^2 + z$muY^2
>     cov_s <- EXYs - EXs * EY
>     var_s <- EX2s - EXs^2
>     r_pool[g] <- cov_s / sqrt(var_s * z$sdY^2)
> 
>     # ---- group-wise imputation: the group's OWN slope fills its own gaps ---
>     ag <- z$EXo - z$beta * z$EYo
>     EXg  <- f * z$EXo + (1 - f) * (ag + z$beta * z$EYm)
>     EX2g <- f * (z$VXo + z$EXo^2) +
>             (1 - f) * (ag^2 + 2 * ag * z$beta * z$EYm + z$beta^2 * z$EY2m + z$resv)
>     EXYg <- f * (z$CovXY + z$EXo * z$EYo) +
>             (1 - f) * (ag * z$EYm + z$beta * z$EY2m)
>     r_group[g] <- (EXYg - EXg * EY) / sqrt((EX2g - EXg^2) * z$sdY^2)
>   }
> 
>   zeta_true <- atanh(groups[[1]]$rho) - atanh(groups[[2]]$rho)

>   zg <- atanh(r_group[1]) - atanh(r_group[2])

> parse_body <- function(txt) {
>   # Markdown soft-wraps a paragraph across source lines, so a single name can
>   # straddle a line break ("crediting von\nHippel (2009)"). Reading line by line
>   # sees a bare "Hippel" and reports it dangling. Join single newlines first;
>   # blank lines are left alone because those are real paragraph breaks.
>   txt <- gsub("(?<=\\S)\n(?=\\S)", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
>   # author string: surnames joined by ", " / ", & " / " and " / " & " / " et al."
>   join <- "(?:,\\s*&\\s*|,\\s*and\\s+|\\s+and\\s+|\\s*&\\s*|,\\s*|\\s+et al\\.\\s*)"
>   # AN APA LETTER SUFFIX IS ALLOWED AFTER THE YEAR, added 2026-10-02. This
>   # required the year to be followed by ")", "," or ";", so "(Shavit, 2026a)"
>   # matched NOTHING -- the body citation was invisible while the reference ENTRY
>   # was seen, because parse_reflist strips the suffix. The result is the worst
>   # shape a checker can have: the entry is read, the citation to it is not, and
>   # the pair reports as an ORPHAN -- "listed but never cited" -- when the body

>   # it is why two agents reached opposite conclusions about whether suffixes work.
>   # The letter is matched but NOT captured, so surname-and-year matching is

>   pat  <- u(paste0("(", SUR, "(?:", join, SUR, ")*(?:", join, ")?)",

> }

>   if (m[1] == -1L) 0L else length(m)
> }
> count_rx <- function(pat, txt) {
>   m <- gregexpr(pat, txt, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
>   if (m[1] == -1L) 0L else length(m)
> }
> measure <- function(path, label) {
>   if (!file.exists(path)) { cat("SKIP ", label, "\n"); return(invisible()) }
>   ln <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
> 
>   # running prose only: drop tables, headings, code fences, block quotes
>   keep <- !grepl("^\\s*(\\||#|>|```|<!--)", ln)
>   prose <- ln[keep]
>   txt <- paste(prose, collapse = "\n")
> 
>   words <- length(strsplit(trimws(gsub("[^[:alnum:] ]", " ", txt)), "\\s+")[[1]])
>   if (words < 100) { cat("SKIP ", label, " (too short)\n"); return(invisible()) }
>   per100 <- function(n) 100 * n / words
> 
>   dash <- per100(count_fixed("\u2014", txt))          # em dash only; en dash is fine
>   bold <- per100(count_rx("\\*\\*[^*]+\\*\\*", txt))
> 
>   paras <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\n[ \t]*\n"))
>   paras <- paras[nchar(paras) > 140]
>   trans <- 100 * sum(grepl(OPENERS, tolower(paras))) / max(1, length(paras))
> 
>   flag <- function(v, t, lower = TRUE)
>     if ((lower && v <= t) || (!lower && v >= t)) "ok  " else "over"
>   cat(sprintf("\n  %s  (%s words of running prose, %d paragraphs)\n",
>               label, format(words, big.mark = ","), length(paras)))
>   cat(sprintf("    %s em-dashes per 100 words  %5.2f   (target <= %.2f; published 0.00)\n",
>               flag(dash, TARGET_DASH), dash, TARGET_DASH))
>   cat(sprintf("    %s bold spans per 100 words %5.2f   (target <= %.2f; published ~0)\n",
>               flag(bold, TARGET_BOLD), bold, TARGET_BOLD))
>   cat(sprintf("    %s paragraphs opening with a transition %4.0f%%   (target >= %d%%)\n",
>               flag(trans, TARGET_TRANS, lower = FALSE), trans, TARGET_TRANS))
>   invisible(c(dash = dash, bold = bold, trans = trans))
> }

> expit <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))

> sel <- function(pi_t, gam = gY) {
>   if (gam == 0) {
>     return(list(po = 1 - pi_t, pm = pi_t, m1o = 0, m2o = 1, m1m = 0, m2m = 1,
>                 A = 1 - pi_t, B = pi_t))
>   }
>   g0 <- uniroot(function(g) I1(function(y) dnorm(y) * expit(g + gam * y)) - pi_t,
>                 c(-40, 40), tol = 1e-14)$root
>   w  <- function(y) expit(g0 + gam * y)
>   pm <- I1(function(y) dnorm(y) * w(y)); po <- 1 - pm
>   list(po = po, pm = pm,
>        m1o = I1(function(y) y * dnorm(y) * (1 - w(y))) / po,
>        m2o = I1(function(y) y^2 * dnorm(y) * (1 - w(y))) / po,
>        m1m = I1(function(y) y * dnorm(y) * w(y)) / pm,
>        m2m = I1(function(y) y^2 * dnorm(y) * w(y)) / pm,
>        A   = I1(function(y) y^2 * dnorm(y) * (1 - w(y))),
>        B   = I1(function(y) y^2 * dnorm(y) * w(y)))
> }
> cov_star <- function(s, r) {

> }

> set.seed(20260801L)
> B1 <- 0.3
> B2 <- 0.4
> SIG <- 1.0
> GAMMA1 <- 0.7
> gen <- function(n) {
>   X <- rnorm(n)
>   data.frame(X = X, Y = B1 * X + B2 * X^2 + rnorm(n, sd = SIG))
> }
> mar_intercept <- function(target, n = 2e5) {
>   d <- gen(n); z <- as.numeric(scale(d$Y))
>   uniroot(function(g0) mean(plogis(g0 + GAMMA1 * z)) - target, c(-12, 12))$root
> }
> impute_joint <- function(x, w, y) {
>   o  <- !is.na(x)
>   Z  <- cbind(1, y)
>   Zo <- Z[o, , drop = FALSE]; Zm <- Z[!o, , drop = FALSE]
>   Yo <- cbind(x[o], w[o])
>   XtXinv <- chol2inv(chol(crossprod(Zo)))
>   Bhat <- XtXinv %*% crossprod(Zo, Yo)
>   E    <- Yo - Zo %*% Bhat
>   S    <- crossprod(E)
>   df   <- nrow(Zo) - ncol(Zo)
>   Sinv <- chol2inv(chol(S))
>   Sig  <- chol2inv(chol(rWishart(1, df, Sinv)[, , 1]))    # inverse-Wishart
>   B    <- Bhat + t(chol(XtXinv)) %*%
>           matrix(rnorm(4), 2, 2) %*% chol(Sig)            # matrix normal
>   nm   <- nrow(Zm)
>   Zm %*% B + matrix(rnorm(nm * 2), nm, 2) %*% chol(Sig)
> }
> GRID <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 401)
> impute_smc <- function(y_mis, b1, b2, s, chunk = 20000L) {
>   out <- numeric(length(y_mis))
>   lp  <- dnorm(GRID, log = TRUE)
>   for (a in seq(1, length(y_mis), by = chunk)) {
>     b   <- min(a + chunk - 1L, length(y_mis))
>     yy  <- y_mis[a:b]
>     mu  <- outer(rep(1, length(yy)), b1 * GRID + b2 * GRID^2)
>     dev <- (yy - mu)
>     lw  <- sweep(-dev^2 / (2 * s^2), 2, lp, "+")
>     # Categorical draw by Gumbel-max rather than inverse-CDF. The first version
>     # used t(apply(W, 1, cumsum)), an R-level loop over 20,000 rows per chunk
>     # run several hundred times, which took the script from an estimated few
>     # minutes to over twenty and still had a cell to go. Gumbel-max is exact,
>     # needs no normalisation and no cumulative sum, and is shift-invariant per
>     # row so the max-subtraction is unnecessary too.
>     g   <- -log(-log(matrix(runif(length(lw)), nrow(lw), ncol(lw))))
>     idx <- max.col(lw + g, ties.method = "first")
>     # jitter within the grid cell so the draw is continuous, not lattice-valued
>     out[a:b] <- GRID[idx] + runif(length(yy), -1, 1) * (GRID[2] - GRID[1]) / 2
>   }
>   out
> }

  the observed cases hold far LESS of the interaction signal than of the
  sample, which is the mechanism behind super-proportional attenuation.
  The observed part does NOT factor: selection depends on (X2, Y), and the
  higher moments involve X2 and Y, so the share is moment-specific.

> }

>              list(muY =  0.9, sdY = 0.7, muX = -0.5, sdX = 0.8, rho = 0.46, gy = 0.2, pm = 0.55))),

> mar_intercept <- function(target, slope = 1.0, Yv, tol = 1e-4) {
>   f <- function(a) mean(plogis(a + slope * Yv)) - target
>   lo <- -20; hi <- 20
>   for (i in 1:200) {
>     mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
>     if (f(mid) > 0) hi <- mid else lo <- mid
>     if (abs(hi - lo) < tol) break
>   }
>   (lo + hi) / 2
> }
> mar_slope <- 1.0
> a_mar     <- mar_intercept(pmiss, mar_slope, d0$Y)
> impose_mar <- function() {
>   p_miss <- plogis(a_mar + mar_slope * d0$Y)
>   miss   <- runif(n) < p_miss
>   # Guard: keep at least enough complete cases to fit the 4-parameter model.
>   if (sum(!miss) < 6L) {
>     keep <- sample(which(miss), 6L - sum(!miss))
>     miss[keep] <- FALSE
>   }
>   d <- d0
>   d$X1[miss] <- NA
>   d
> }

> suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(source("R/simulation_functions.R")))
> set.seed(77)
> p <- default_params()
> p$beta3 <- 0
> b1<-p$beta1
> rho<-p$rho
> sig<-p$sigma
> pi_t <- 0.40
> OI <- list(blue="#0072B2", verm="#D55E00", green="#009E73", orange="#E69F00",
>            ink="#1a1a1a", grey="#8a8a8a")
> Vu <- sig^2*(1-rho^2)/(b1^2*(1-rho^2)+sig^2)
> run_mech <- function(gz2, gzy, N=5e5) {
>   pp <- p; pp$gamma_z2 <- gz2; pp$gamma_zy <- gzy
>   d <- generate_data(N, pp)
>   if (gz2==0 && gzy==0) mis <- runif(N) < pi_t
>   else { mf <- calibrate_mar(pi_t, pp, n_ref=2e5); mis <- is.na(mf(d)$X1) }
>   cc <- lm(X1 ~ X2 + Y, data=d[!mis,])
>   x1 <- d$X1; x1[mis] <- predict(cc, newdata=d[mis,])
>   delta <- mean((!mis)*d$X2)
>   kap   <- mean((!mis)*d$X2^2)
>   Vw    <- 1 + rho^2 - Vu*(1-kap)
>   a1    <- b1*(1-rho^2)/(1 - pi_t*Vu - rho^2 - (delta*Vu)^2/Vw)
>   list(delta=delta,
>        plim = unname(coef(lm(d$Y ~ x1*d$X2))[4]),
>        form = -(delta*Vu/Vw)*a1,
>        mis  = mis, X2 = d$X2)
> }
> mechs <- list(
>   MCAR       = run_mech(0,   0),
>   `X2-only`  = run_mech(0.7, 0),
>   `Y-only`   = run_mech(0,   0.7),

> suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(source("R/simulation_functions.R")))
> set.seed(2607)
> rho1 <- 0.6
> rho2 <- 0.2
> pi_t <- 0.40
> gy <- 0.7
> N <- 400
> OI <- list(blue = "#0072B2", verm = "#D55E00", ink = "#1a1a1a",
>            grey = "#8a8a8a", faint = "#d9d9d9")
> n1 <- N/2
> G   <- rep(1:2, each = n1)
> rho <- ifelse(G == 1, rho1, rho2)
> y   <- rnorm(N)
> x   <- rho * y + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N)
> g0  <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + gy * rnorm(2e5))) - pi_t, c(-30, 30))$root
> mis <- runif(N) < plogis(g0 + gy * y)
> fp  <- lm(x[!mis] ~ y[!mis] + factor(G[!mis]))
> b_p <- coef(fp)[2]
> s_p <- sigma(fp)
> xp  <- x
> xp[mis] <- coef(fp)[1] + ifelse(G[mis] == 2, coef(fp)[3], 0) +
>            b_p * y[mis] + s_p * rnorm(sum(mis))
> xg <- x
> slopes_g <- numeric(2)
> for (gg in 1:2) {
>   idx <- G == gg; obs <- idx & !mis; mm <- idx & mis
>   f <- lm(x[obs] ~ y[obs]); slopes_g[gg] <- coef(f)[2]
>   xg[mm] <- coef(f)[1] + coef(f)[2] * y[mm] + sigma(f) * rnorm(sum(mm))
> }
> zof <- function(v) atanh(cor(v[G==1], y[G==1])) - atanh(cor(v[G==2], y[G==2]))
> z_full <- zof(x)
> z_pool <- zof(xp)
> z_grp <- zof(xg)
> png("results/sequel_mech_slopes.png", width = 1873, height = 807, res = 288)
> layout(matrix(c(1,2,3,4,4,4), 2, 3, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(3.1, 1))
> par(family = "sans", col.axis = OI$ink, fg = OI$ink, cex.axis = .76)
> panel <- function(xv, ttl, sub, imputed_open, show_pooled = FALSE) {
>   par(mar = c(2.9, 2.9, 3.4, 0.6))
>   plot(NA, xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(-3.2, 3.2), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
>   abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = OI$faint, lwd = 1, lty = 3)
>   for (gg in 1:2) {
>     col <- if (gg == 1) OI$blue else OI$verm
>     idx <- G == gg
>     # observed = filled, imputed = open
>     points(y[idx & !mis], xv[idx & !mis], pch = 19, cex = .5,
>            col = adjustcolor(col, .55))
>     if (imputed_open)
>       points(y[idx & mis], xv[idx & mis], pch = 21, cex = .55,
>              col = col, bg = "white", lwd = .9)
>     f <- lm(xv[idx] ~ y[idx])
>     abline(f, col = col, lwd = 2.6)
>   }
>   if (show_pooled) {                      # the single slope used to fill BOTH groups
>     abline(a = coef(fp)[1], b = b_p, col = OI$ink, lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
>     text(-2.9, 2.65, "one pooled slope\nfills both groups", adj = 0, cex = .62,
>          col = OI$ink)
>   }
>   axis(1, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = .8, col.ticks = OI$grey)
>   axis(2, las = 1, lwd = 0, lwd.ticks = .8, col.ticks = OI$grey)
>   mtext("Y", side = 1, line = 1.8, cex = .76)
>   mtext("X", side = 2, line = 1.8, cex = .76)
>   mtext(ttl, side = 3, line = 1.9, adj = 0, cex = .86, col = OI$ink)
>   for (i in seq_along(sub))

> }
> panel(x,  "A. Complete data",        "two genuinely different slopes", FALSE)

> source("R/simulation_functions.R")
> set.seed(20260804L + 313L)
> N <- 5e5
> M <- 5L
> PI <- 0.40
> REPS <- 24L
> GAMMA1 <- 0.7
> predictors <- function(b1, b2, s) {
>   VarY <- b1^2 + 2 * b2^2 + s^2
>   c(rho2 = b1^2 / VarY,
>     r    = (b1 / VarY)^2 * (8 * b2^3 + 6 * b1^2 * b2) / (2 * b2))
> }
> mar_intercept <- function(b1, b2, s, target, n = 2e5) {
>   x <- rnorm(n); y <- b1 * x + b2 * x^2 + rnorm(n, sd = s)
>   z <- as.numeric(scale(y))
>   uniroot(function(g0) mean(plogis(g0 + GAMMA1 * z)) - target, c(-12, 12))$root
> }
> kappa_at <- function(b1, b2, sig, mech = c("MAR", "MCAR"), reps = REPS) {
>   mech <- match.arg(mech)
>   g0 <- if (mech == "MAR") mar_intercept(b1, b2, sig, PI) else NA_real_
>   k <- numeric(reps)
>   for (rep in seq_len(reps)) {
>     X <- rnorm(N); Y <- b1 * X + b2 * X^2 + rnorm(N, sd = sig)
>     miss <- if (mech == "MAR")
>       runif(N) < plogis(g0 + GAMMA1 * as.numeric(scale(Y))) else runif(N) < PI
>     if (all(miss)) miss[1] <- FALSE
>     d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y); d$X[miss] <- NA
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>     est <- numeric(M)
>     for (j in seq_len(M)) {
>       dd <- d; dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>       est[j] <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq,
>                                data = transform(dd, Xsq = X^2)))["Xsq"])
>     }
>     k[rep] <- 1 - mean(est) / b2
>   }
>   c(kappa = mean(k), mcse = sd(k) / sqrt(reps))
> }
> CONFIGS <- list(
>   list(l = "base            b1=0.3 b2=0.4  s=1.0", b1 = 0.3, b2 = 0.4,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "no linear term  b1=0.0 b2=0.4  s=1.0", b1 = 0.0, b2 = 0.4,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "strong linear   b1=1.0 b2=0.4  s=1.0", b1 = 1.0, b2 = 0.4,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "linear dominant b1=1.5 b2=0.1  s=1.0", b1 = 1.5, b2 = 0.1,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "square dominant b1=0.1 b2=1.5  s=1.0", b1 = 0.1, b2 = 1.5,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "low noise       b1=0.3 b2=0.4  s=0.5", b1 = 0.3, b2 = 0.4,  s = 0.5),
>   list(l = "S2 spread       b1=1.2 b2=0.5  s=1.0", b1 = 1.2, b2 = 0.5,  s = 1.0),
>   list(l = "S3 spread       b1=0.5 b2=0.5  s=0.3", b1 = 0.5, b2 = 0.5,  s = 0.3),
>   # discriminating pair: rho^2 ranks A above B, r ranks B above A
>   list(l = "A1 discriminating b1=0.6 b2=0.2 s=2.0", b1 = 0.6, b2 = 0.2, s = 2.0),
>   list(l = "B1 discriminating b1=0.3 b2=1.2 s=0.5", b1 = 0.3, b2 = 1.2, s = 0.5)
> )
> cat(sprintf("MAR on Y (logistic, slope %.1f), pi = %.2f, N = %.0e, %d reps\n\n",

> source("R/simulation_functions.R")
> set.seed(20260804L)
> N <- 5e5

> M <- 5L
> PI <- 0.40
> kappa_at <- function(b1, b2, sig, pi_t = PI, reps = REPS) {
>   k <- numeric(reps)
>   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>     X <- rnorm(N)
>     Y <- b1 * X + b2 * X^2 + rnorm(N, sd = sig)
>     d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y)
>     d$X[runif(N) < pi_t] <- NA                     # MCAR: isolates the design
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>     est <- numeric(M)
>     for (j in seq_len(M)) {
>       dd <- d; dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>       est[j] <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq,
>                                data = transform(dd, Xsq = X^2)))["Xsq"])
>     }
>     k[r] <- 1 - mean(est) / b2
>   }
>   c(kappa = mean(k), mcse = sd(k) / sqrt(reps))
> }
> predictors <- function(b1, b2, s) {
>   VarY <- b1^2 + 2 * b2^2 + s^2
>   rho2 <- b1^2 / VarY
>   lam  <- b1 / VarY
>   m3   <- 8 * b2^3 + 6 * b1^2 * b2
>   c(rho2 = rho2, r = lam^2 * m3 / (2 * b2))
> }
> CONFIGS <- list(
>   # -- pair 1: rho^2 ranks A1 well above B1; r ranks B1 above A1 --

>   n <- length(y); p <- 3L
>   s2 <- sum(r^2) / (n - p)

>   c(est = unname(b[3]), se = sqrt(v))
> }

> mi_arm <- function(y, x, jav) {
>   obs <- !is.na(x)
>   P   <- cbind(1, y)
>   Q <- numeric(M); U <- numeric(M)
>   w  <- x^2                                  # NA wherever x is

>     xj <- x

>     xj[!obs] <- P[!obs, , drop = FALSE] %*% d1$beta +

>     if (jav) {

>       wj[!obs] <- P[!obs, , drop = FALSE] %*% d2$beta +

>       X <- cbind(1, xj, wj)
>       q <- qr(X); b <- qr.coef(q, y); r <- y - X %*% b

>     } else {
>       f <- b2_fit(y, xj)
>       Q[j] <- f["est"]; U[j] <- f["se"]^2
>     }
>   }

> }

> gh <- function(n) {
>   k <- 1:(n - 1)
>   J <- matrix(0, n, n)
>   J[cbind(k, k + 1)] <- sqrt(k); J[cbind(k + 1, k)] <- sqrt(k)
>   e <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
>   list(x = rev(e$values), w = rev(e$vectors[1, ]^2))
> }
> build <- function(b1, b2, sg, b0 = 0, nq = 16) {
>   Q <- gh(nq)
>   Yf <- function(x, e) b0 + b1 * x + b2 * x^2 + e
>   EE <- function(f) {
>     s <- 0
>     for (i in seq_along(Q$x)) for (j in seq_along(Q$x))
>       s <- s + Q$w[i] * Q$w[j] * f(Q$x[i], sg * Q$x[j])
>     s
>   }
>   EY   <- EE(function(x, e) Yf(x, e))
>   varY <- EE(function(x, e) Yf(x, e)^2) - EY^2
>   gam  <- EE(function(x, e) x * Yf(x, e)) / varY
>   alp  <- -gam * EY
>   tau2 <- 1 - gam^2 * varY
>   Ec <- function(pz, py) EE(function(x, e) x^pz * Yf(x, e)^py)
>   Ei <- function(pz, py) {
>     s <- 0
>     for (i in seq_along(Q$x)) for (j in seq_along(Q$x)) for (k in seq_along(Q$x)) {
>       y <- Yf(Q$x[i], sg * Q$x[j])
>       z <- alp + gam * y + sqrt(max(tau2, 0)) * Q$x[k]
>       s <- s + Q$w[i] * Q$w[j] * Q$w[k] * z^pz * y^py
>     }
>     s
>   }
>   Gm <- function(f) matrix(c(f(0, 0), f(1, 0), f(2, 0),
>                              f(1, 0), f(2, 0), f(3, 0),
>                              f(2, 0), f(3, 0), f(4, 0)), 3, 3)
>   wv <- function(f) c(f(0, 1), f(1, 1), f(2, 1))
>   list(G = Gm(Ec), Gi = Gm(Ei), om = wv(Ec), omi = wv(Ei), b2 = b2,
>        Ec = Ec, Ei = Ei)
> }
> kappa_of <- function(M) function(p) {
>   A <- (1 - p) * M$G + p * M$Gi
>   r <- (1 - p) * M$om + p * M$omi
>   1 - solve(A, r)[3] / M$b2
> }

> source("R/simulation_functions.R")
> set.seed(20260801L)
> N <- 5e5
> REPS <- 6L
> M <- 5L
> PI <- 0.40
> lambda_of <- function(b1, b2, sig) b1^2 / (b1^2 + 2 * b2^2 + sig^2)
> kappa_at <- function(b1, b2, sig, reps = REPS) {
>   k <- numeric(reps)
>   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>     X <- rnorm(N)
>     Y <- b1 * X + b2 * X^2 + rnorm(N, sd = sig)
>     d <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y)
>     d$X[runif(N) < PI] <- NA
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>     est <- numeric(M)
>     for (j in seq_len(M)) {
>       dd <- d; dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>       est[j] <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq,
>                                data = transform(dd, Xsq = X^2)))["Xsq"])
>     }
>     k[r] <- 1 - mean(est) / b2
>   }
>   c(kappa = mean(k), mcse = sd(k) / sqrt(reps))
> }
> run <- function(label, group, b1, b2, sig) {
>   r <- kappa_at(b1, b2, sig)
>   lam <- lambda_of(b1, b2, sig)
>   cat(sprintf("  %-26s lambda %.4f   kappa %.4f (%.4f)   c = kappa/pi %.4f\n",
>               label, lam, r["kappa"], r["mcse"], r["kappa"] / PI))
>   data.frame(label = label, group = group, b1 = b1, b2 = b2, sigma = sig,
>              lambda = lam, kappa = unname(r["kappa"]), mcse = unname(r["mcse"]),
>              c = unname(r["kappa"]) / PI, N = N, reps = REPS,
>              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> }
> rows <- list()
> cat("--- sweep in b1 (b2 = 0.4, sigma = 1): the shape of c against lambda ---\n")

> source("R/simulation_functions.R")
> set.seed(20260801L)
> B0 <- 0.0
> B1 <- 0.3
> B2 <- 0.4
> SIG <- 1.0
> GAMMA1 <- 0.7
> gen <- function(n) {
>   X <- rnorm(n)
>   Y <- B0 + B1 * X + B2 * X^2 + rnorm(n, sd = SIG)
>   data.frame(X = X, Y = Y)
> }
> mar_intercept <- function(target, n = 2e5) {
>   d <- gen(n); z <- as.numeric(scale(d$Y))
>   f <- function(g0) mean(plogis(g0 + GAMMA1 * z)) - target
>   uniroot(f, c(-12, 12))$root
> }
> drop_mar <- function(d, g0) {
>   z <- as.numeric(scale(d$Y))
>   miss <- runif(nrow(d)) < plogis(g0 + GAMMA1 * z)
>   d$X[miss] <- NA
>   d
> }
> drop_mcar <- function(d, rate) {
>   d$X[runif(nrow(d)) < rate] <- NA
>   d
> }
> b2_of <- function(fit) unname(coef(fit)["Xsq"])
> arm_full <- function(d) b2_of(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq, data = transform(d, Xsq = X^2)))
> arm_listwise <- function(d) {
>   o <- d[!is.na(d$X), ]
>   b2_of(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq, data = transform(o, Xsq = X^2)))
> }
> arm_naive <- function(d, m = 5L) {
>   P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>   est <- numeric(m)
>   for (j in seq_len(m)) {
>     dd <- d
>     dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>     est[j] <- b2_of(lm(Y ~ X + Xsq, data = transform(dd, Xsq = X^2)))
>   }
>   mean(est)
> }
> arm_jav <- function(d, m = 5L) {
>   d$W <- d$X^2                      # NA wherever X is
>   P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d)
>   est <- numeric(m)
>   for (j in seq_len(m)) {
>     dd <- d
>     dd$X[is.na(d$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$X, P)
>     dd$W[is.na(d$W)] <- impute_norm_draw(d$W, P)
>     est[j] <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ X + W, data = dd))["W"])
>   }
>   mean(est)
> }
> N    <- 5e5
> REPS <- 10L
> RATES <- c(0.20, 0.40)
> g0 <- vapply(RATES, mar_intercept, numeric(1))

MAR logistic intercepts: -1.5194 (20%), -0.4412 (40%)
> rows <- list()
> for (i in seq_along(RATES)) {
>   rate <- RATES[i]
>   for (mech in c("MAR", "MCAR")) {
>     acc <- matrix(NA_real_, REPS, 4,
>                   dimnames = list(NULL, c("full", "listwise", "naive", "jav")))
>     realised <- numeric(REPS)
>     for (r in seq_len(REPS)) {

> suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(source("R/simulation_functions.R")))
> set.seed(20260725)
> rho1 <- 0.6
> rho2 <- 0.2
> zeta <- atanh(rho1) - atanh(rho2)
> pi_t <- 0.40
> m_imp <- 20L
> reps <- 300L
> Ns   <- c(40, 80, 160, 320)
> gen <- function(N) {
>   n1 <- N %/% 2; n2 <- N - n1
>   g  <- rep(c(1, 2), c(n1, n2))
>   rho <- ifelse(g == 1, rho1, rho2)
>   x  <- rnorm(N)
>   y  <- rho * x + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N)   # X,Y ~ BVN(0,1,rho_g)
>   data.frame(X = x, Y = y, G = g)
> }
> yref <- rnorm(2e5)
> g0 <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + 0.7 * yref)) - pi_t, c(-20, 20))$root
> impose <- function(d) { d$X[runif(nrow(d)) < plogis(g0 + 0.7 * d$Y)] <- NA; d }
> zdiff <- function(d) {
>   r1 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 1], d$Y[d$G == 1], use = "complete.obs"))
>   r2 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 2], d$Y[d$G == 2], use = "complete.obs"))
>   n1 <- sum(d$G == 1 & !is.na(d$X)); n2 <- sum(d$G == 2 & !is.na(d$X))
>   if (n1 < 5 || n2 < 5 || abs(r1) >= 1 || abs(r2) >= 1) return(NULL)
>   est <- atanh(r1) - atanh(r2)
>   se  <- sqrt(1/(n1 - 3) + 1/(n2 - 3))
>   c(est = est, se = se)
> }
> wald <- function(est, se, true) {
>   est <- unname(est); se <- unname(se)
>   lo <- est - 1.96 * se; hi <- est + 1.96 * se
>   c(est = est, covered = as.numeric(true >= lo & true <= hi),
>     reject = as.numeric(lo > 0 | hi < 0))
> }
> mi_arm <- function(dm, congenial) {
>   Q <- U <- numeric(m_imp)
>   for (j in seq_len(m_imp)) {
>     d <- dm
>     if (congenial) {
>       for (gg in 1:2) {
>         idx <- d$G == gg
>         if (any(is.na(d$X[idx]))) {
>           P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d[idx, ])
>           d$X[idx][is.na(dm$X[idx])] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X[idx], P)
>         }
>       }
>     } else {
>       P <- model.matrix(~ Y + factor(G), data = d)   # group MAIN EFFECT only
>       d$X[is.na(dm$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X, P)
>     }
>     v <- zdiff(d); if (is.null(v)) return(NULL)
>     Q[j] <- v["est"]; U[j] <- v["se"]^2
>   }
>   pool_rubin(Q, U, df_com = nrow(dm) - 6, true = zeta)
> }
> rows <- list()
> k <- 0L
> for (N in Ns) {
>   acc <- list(full = c(), listw = c(), naive = c(), cong = c())
>   cov <- list(full = c(), listw = c(), naive = c(), cong = c())
>   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>     d0 <- gen(N); dm <- impose(d0)
>     vf <- zdiff(d0)
>     if (!is.null(vf)) { w <- wald(vf["est"], vf["se"], zeta)
>       acc$full <- c(acc$full, w["est"]); cov$full <- c(cov$full, w["covered"]) }
>     vl <- zdiff(dm)
>     if (!is.null(vl)) { w <- wald(vl["est"], vl["se"], zeta)
>       acc$listw <- c(acc$listw, w["est"]); cov$listw <- c(cov$listw, w["covered"]) }
>     vn <- tryCatch(mi_arm(dm, congenial = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
>     if (!is.null(vn)) { acc$naive <- c(acc$naive, vn["est"])
>       cov$naive <- c(cov$naive, vn["covered"]) }
>     vc <- tryCatch(mi_arm(dm, congenial = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
>     if (!is.null(vc)) { acc$cong <- c(acc$cong, vc["est"])
>       cov$cong <- c(cov$cong, vc["covered"]) }
>   }
>   for (arm in names(acc)) {
>     k <- k + 1L; n <- length(acc[[arm]])
>     rows[[k]] <- data.frame(N = N, arm = arm, n_valid = n,
>       bias_z = mean(acc[[arm]]) - zeta,
>       mcse   = sd(acc[[arm]])/sqrt(n),
>       coverage = mean(cov[[arm]]))
>   }
>   cat(sprintf("N=%d done\n", N))
> }

>   # Evaluated with zeta_plim_exact(): the Monte Carlo evaluator's noise floor

closed-form curve already present, skipping
> gen <- function(N) {
>   n1 <- N %/% 2; n2 <- N - n1
>   G  <- rep(c(1, 2), c(n1, n2))
>   rho <- ifelse(G == 1, r1, r2)
>   y <- rnorm(N)
>   data.frame(X = rho * y + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(N), Y = y, G = G)
> }
> zdiff <- function(d) {
>   a <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 1], d$Y[d$G == 1], use = "complete.obs"))
>   b <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 2], d$Y[d$G == 2], use = "complete.obs"))
>   k1 <- sum(d$G == 1 & !is.na(d$X)); k2 <- sum(d$G == 2 & !is.na(d$X))
>   if (k1 < 5 || k2 < 5 || !is.finite(a) || !is.finite(b) ||
>       abs(a) >= 1 || abs(b) >= 1) return(NULL)
>   c(est = unname(atanh(a) - atanh(b)),
>     se  = unname(sqrt(1 / (k1 - 3) + 1 / (k2 - 3))))
> }
> mi_arm <- function(dm, groupwise) {
>   Q <- U <- numeric(m_imp)
>   for (j in seq_len(m_imp)) {
>     d <- dm
>     if (groupwise) {
>       for (gg in 1:2) {
>         idx <- d$G == gg
>         if (any(is.na(dm$X[idx]))) {
>           P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d[idx, ])
>           d$X[idx][is.na(dm$X[idx])] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X[idx], P)
>         }
>       }
>     } else {
>       P <- model.matrix(~ Y + factor(G), data = d)
>       d$X[is.na(dm$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X, P)
>     }
>     v <- zdiff(d); if (is.null(v)) return(NULL)
>     Q[j] <- v["est"]; U[j] <- v["se"]^2
>   }
>   pool_rubin(Q, U, df_com = nrow(dm) - 6, true = zeta)
> }
> t0 <- Sys.time()
> for (pi_t in pis) {
>   ck <- sprintf("results/sequel_kappa_curve_p%02d.csv", round(100 * pi_t))
>   if (file.exists(ck)) { cat("skip (checkpoint):", ck, "\n"); next }
>   yref <- rnorm(2e5)
>   g0 <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + 0.7 * yref)) - pi_t, c(-30, 30))$root
> 
>   rows <- list(); k <- 0L
>   for (N in Ns) {
>     acc <- list(MI_pooled = list(), MI_groupwise = list())
>     for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>       d0 <- gen(N)
>       dm <- d0; dm$X[runif(N) < plogis(g0 + 0.7 * d0$Y)] <- NA
>       for (arm in names(acc)) {
>         v <- tryCatch(mi_arm(dm, arm == "MI_groupwise"), error = function(e) NULL)
>         if (!is.null(v)) acc[[arm]][[length(acc[[arm]]) + 1]] <-
>           c(est = unname(v["est"]), covered = unname(v["covered"]))
>       }
>     }
>     for (arm in names(acc)) {
>       M <- do.call(rbind, acc[[arm]]); if (is.null(M) || !nrow(M)) next
>       n <- nrow(M); est <- M[, "est"]
>       k <- k + 1L
>       rows[[k]] <- data.frame(
>         pi = pi_t, N = N, arm = arm, n_valid = n, zeta = zeta,

>         mcse_bias = sd(est) / sqrt(n),

>         coverage = mean(M[, "covered"]),
>         mcse_cov = sqrt(mean(M[, "covered"]) * (1 - mean(M[, "covered"])) / n))

>     cat(sprintf("[pi=%.2f] N=%d done (%.1f min)\n", pi_t, N,

> suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(source("R/simulation_functions.R")))
> source("R/drv004_general.R")
> set.seed(20260726)
> args   <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
> reps   <- if (length(args) >= 1) as.integer(args[1]) else 1000L
> m_imp  <- 20L
> rho_c  <- 0.40
> Ns     <- c(80, 160, 320, 640)
> ratios <- c(1, 1.5, 2, 3)
> pis    <- c(0.20, 0.40)
> gen <- function(N, ratio) {
>   G <- rep(1:2, each = N %/% 2)
>   sdY <- ifelse(G == 1, 1, ratio)
>   Y <- rnorm(length(G), 0, sdY)
>   X <- rho_c * (Y / sdY) + sqrt(1 - rho_c^2) * rnorm(length(G))
>   data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, G = G)
> }
> zdiff <- function(d) {
>   r1 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 1], d$Y[d$G == 1], use = "complete.obs"))
>   r2 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 2], d$Y[d$G == 2], use = "complete.obs"))
>   n1 <- sum(d$G == 1 & !is.na(d$X)); n2 <- sum(d$G == 2 & !is.na(d$X))
>   if (n1 < 5 || n2 < 5 || !is.finite(r1) || !is.finite(r2) ||
>       abs(r1) >= 1 || abs(r2) >= 1) return(NULL)
>   c(est = unname(atanh(r1) - atanh(r2)),
>     se  = unname(sqrt(1 / (n1 - 3) + 1 / (n2 - 3))))
> }
> impute <- function(dm, groupwise) {
>   d <- dm
>   if (groupwise) {
>     for (g in 1:2) {
>       i <- d$G == g
>       if (any(is.na(dm$X[i]))) {
>         P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d[i, ])
>         d$X[i][is.na(dm$X[i])] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X[i], P)
>       }
>     }
>   } else {
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y + factor(G), data = d)
>     d$X[is.na(dm$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X, P)
>   }
>   d
> }
> mi_arm <- function(dm, groupwise) {
>   Q <- U <- numeric(m_imp)
>   for (j in seq_len(m_imp)) {
>     v <- zdiff(impute(dm, groupwise)); if (is.null(v)) return(NULL)
>     Q[j] <- v["est"]; U[j] <- v["se"]^2
>   }
>   pool_rubin(Q, U, df_com = nrow(dm) - 6, true = 0)
> }
> t0 <- Sys.time()
> for (ratio in ratios) for (pi_t in pis) {
>   ck <- sprintf("results/manuf_r%02d_p%02d.csv", round(10 * ratio), round(100 * pi_t))
>   if (file.exists(ck)) { cat("skip:", ck, "\n"); next }
> 
>   # closed-form prediction for this cell
>   gr <- list(list(muY = 0, sdY = 1, muX = 0, sdX = 1, rho = rho_c,
>                   sel = mk_sel(0, 1, 0.7, pi_t)),
>              list(muY = 0, sdY = ratio, muX = 0, sdX = 1, rho = rho_c,
>                   sel = mk_sel(0, ratio, 0.7, pi_t)))
>   pred <- drv004_general(gr)$zeta_pooled
> 
>   rows <- list(); k <- 0L
>   for (N in Ns) {
>     acc <- list(listwise = list(), MI_pooled = list(), MI_groupwise = list())
>     for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
>       d <- gen(N, ratio)
>       mis <- logical(nrow(d))
>       for (g in 1:2) {
>         i <- d$G == g
>         a <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + 0.7 * d$Y[i])) - pi_t, c(-40, 40))$root
>         mis[i] <- runif(sum(i)) < plogis(a + 0.7 * d$Y[i])
>       }
>       dm <- d; dm$X[mis] <- NA
>       vl <- zdiff(dm)
>       if (!is.null(vl)) {
>         lo <- vl["est"] - 1.96 * vl["se"]; hi <- vl["est"] + 1.96 * vl["se"]
>         acc$listwise[[length(acc$listwise) + 1]] <-
>           c(est = unname(vl["est"]), covered = as.numeric(0 >= lo & 0 <= hi),
>             reject = as.numeric(lo > 0 | hi < 0))
>       }
>       for (arm in c("MI_pooled", "MI_groupwise")) {
>         v <- tryCatch(mi_arm(dm, arm == "MI_groupwise"), error = function(e) NULL)
>         if (!is.null(v)) acc[[arm]][[length(acc[[arm]]) + 1]] <-
>           c(est = unname(v["est"]), covered = unname(v["covered"]),

>       }

>     for (arm in names(acc)) {

>       k <- k + 1L
>       rows[[k]] <- data.frame(

> suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(source("R/simulation_functions.R")))
> set.seed(20260725)
> args  <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
> Npop  <- if (length(args) >= 1) as.numeric(args[1]) else 2e6
> reps  <- if (length(args) >= 2) as.integer(args[2]) else 1000L
> m_imp <- 20L
> rho_c <- 0.40
> pi_t  <- 0.40
> gen <- function(N, r1 = rho_c, r2 = rho_c) {
>   G   <- rep(1:2, each = N %/% 2)
>   rho <- ifelse(G == 1, r1, r2)
>   y <- rnorm(length(G))
>   data.frame(X = rho * y + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(length(G)), Y = y, G = G)
> }
> calib <- function(lin, target) {
>   uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + lin)) - target, c(-40, 40))$root
> }
> mechanisms <- list(
>   `1 MAR-Y` = function(d) {
>     a <- calib(0.7 * d$Y, pi_t); runif(nrow(d)) < plogis(a + 0.7 * d$Y)
>   },
>   `2 MNAR-X` = function(d) {
>     a <- calib(0.7 * d$X, pi_t); runif(nrow(d)) < plogis(a + 0.7 * d$X)
>   },
>   `3 MNAR-X asym` = function(d) {
>     out <- logical(nrow(d))
>     for (g in 1:2) {
>       i <- d$G == g
>       lin <- if (g == 1) 1.2 * d$X[i] else rep(0, sum(i))   # group 2 = MCAR
>       a <- calib(lin, pi_t)                                  # SAME rate per group
>       out[i] <- runif(sum(i)) < plogis(a + lin)
>     }
>     out
>   },
>   `4 MNAR-X opposite` = function(d) {
>     out <- logical(nrow(d))
>     for (g in 1:2) {
>       i <- d$G == g
>       lin <- (if (g == 1) 1.2 else -1.2) * d$X[i]
>       a <- calib(lin, pi_t)
>       out[i] <- runif(sum(i)) < plogis(a + lin)
>     }
>     out
>   }
> )
> zdiff <- function(d) {
>   r1 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 1], d$Y[d$G == 1], use = "complete.obs"))
>   r2 <- suppressWarnings(cor(d$X[d$G == 2], d$Y[d$G == 2], use = "complete.obs"))
>   n1 <- sum(d$G == 1 & !is.na(d$X)); n2 <- sum(d$G == 2 & !is.na(d$X))
>   if (n1 < 5 || n2 < 5 || !is.finite(r1) || !is.finite(r2) ||
>       abs(r1) >= 1 || abs(r2) >= 1) return(NULL)
>   c(est = unname(atanh(r1) - atanh(r2)),
>     se  = unname(sqrt(1 / (n1 - 3) + 1 / (n2 - 3))))
> }
> impute <- function(dm, groupwise) {
>   d <- dm
>   if (groupwise) {
>     for (g in 1:2) {
>       i <- d$G == g
>       if (any(is.na(dm$X[i]))) {
>         P <- model.matrix(~ Y, data = d[i, ])
>         d$X[i][is.na(dm$X[i])] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X[i], P)
>       }
>     }
>   } else {
>     P <- model.matrix(~ Y + factor(G), data = d)
>     d$X[is.na(dm$X)] <- impute_norm_draw(dm$X, P)
>   }
>   d
> }

> FAILS <- 0L

> grab <- function(file, regex) {
>   if (!file.exists(file)) return(NA_real_)
>   txt <- paste(readLines(file, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
>   m <- regexec(regex, txt, perl = TRUE)
>   parts <- regmatches(txt, m)[[1]]
>   if (!length(parts)) return(NA_real_)
>   # group 1 if the regex defines one, else the whole match
>   target <- if (length(parts) >= 2) parts[2] else parts[1]
>   num <- regmatches(target, regexpr("[-+]?[0-9]*\\.?[0-9]+", target))
>   if (!length(num)) return(NA_real_)
>   as.numeric(num[1])
> }
> chk <- function(label, file, regex, canonical, tol = 5e-4) {
>   # A canonical that comes back empty -- a mistyped column name, a filter that
>   # matches no row -- used to reach `if (abs(got - canonical) <= tol)` with a
>   # zero-length value and abort the ENTIRE suite with "argument is of length
>   # zero", losing every check after it. A broken guard must report itself, not
>   # take the other 120 down with it. Found 2026-08-04 by writing one.
>   if (length(canonical) != 1L || is.na(canonical)) {
>     FAILS <<- FAILS + 1L
>     cat(sprintf("  FAIL     %-58s  canonical is empty (bad column or filter)\n",
>                 label))
>     return(invisible())
>   }
>   got <- grab(file, regex)
>   if (is.na(got)) {
>     MISSING <<- MISSING + 1L
>     cat(sprintf("  MISSING  %-58s  pattern not found in %s\n", label, basename(file)))
>     return(invisible())
>   }
>   if (abs(got - canonical) <= tol) {
>     PASSES <<- PASSES + 1L
>     cat(sprintf("  ok       %-58s  %.4f\n", label, got))
>   } else {
>     FAILS <<- FAILS + 1L
>     cat(sprintf("  FAIL     %-58s  artifact %.4f  vs canonical %.4f\n",
>                 label, got, canonical))
>   }
> }

os.chdir() in the code

1 script calls os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

f(rho, v) = rho*sqrt(v)/sqrt(rho**2*v - rho**2 + 1)
f is odd in rho: True

SUFFICIENCY: h(r1) - h(r1) = 0   identically in v  ->  rho_1 = rho_2 suffices, by an identity,
  so any numeric check of it is NON-DISCRIMINATING.

NECESSITY, via the derivative:
  sympy  h'(rho) = (rho**2*v - rho**2 - sqrt(v)*sqrt(rho**2*v - rho**2 + 1) + 1)/(rho**4*v - rho**4 - rho**2*v + 2*rho**2 - 1)
  claimed form   = (sqrt(v) - sqrt(-rho**2*(1 - v) + 1))/((1 - rho**2)*sqrt(-rho**2*(1 - v) + 1))
  difference simplifies to: 0
  identical: True

  sqrt(v) - D has the sign of v - 1, because
    v - D^2 = v - 1 + rho^2 (1 - v) = -(1 - v)(1 - rho^2): True
  so for 0 < v < 1 and |rho| < 1, v - D^2 < 0, hence sqrt(v) < D and h' < 0.
  h is STRICTLY DECREASING on (-1, 1), therefore injective, therefore
  bias = h(rho_1) - h(rho_2) = 0  <=>  rho_1 = rho_2.  NECESSARY AND SUFFICIENT.

Ethics Approval Check

An ethics approval statement was detected, based on the following text:

Ethics approval.

StatCheck

No t-tests or F-tests detected.

The accuracy of StatCheck has only been validated for t-tests and F-tests.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script.
