The Appendix drops all three and restates the boundary in the form the algebra actually supportsif the groups share both the slope β_g and the residual variance τ²_g, then a zero contrast stays zero: ζ = 0 ⟹ plim ζ = 0, for any selection on Y.

Those two conditions are sufficient, and -once the missing rate varies -necessary: for two groups the contrast survives at every rate only when the slope is shared and the residual variance is too, with the one trivial exception that neither group has any association at all. That holds for any positive group shares and any positive outcome variances, equal or not (Appendix). The Appendix also records the object underneath both statements: under missingness completely at random the pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate, so the bias is the imputed rows' failure to satisfy the analysis's own normal equations. That failure being zero is normal-equation compatibility, which is weaker than congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense. A correlation is a ratio of those moments rather than a coefficient in them, which is why this paper's estimand needs the further step the Appendix takes by hand. The special case makes the two look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations; §Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart.

The assumptions, and what fails without each

Assumed

Where it is used What happens without it Missingness depends on Y only Step 1 E[X|Y,R=1] ≠ ρ_g•Y, so the observed part no longer carries ρ_g cleanly and the complete-case slope becomes biased as well. Selection on Y already biases the complete-case correlation: it shrinks Var(Y | R=1) to 0.907 at 40% missing and range-restricts each group's correlation with it, which displaces the contrast by -0.019 ( §Results 1) Within-group bivariate normality Steps 1, 5 the conditional mean may be non-linear; the pooled-slope mechanism survives, the closed form does not Equal groups, common Y distribution, symmetric selection Steps 3-6 of the special case only superseded by §"The general form", which drops all of it: b becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes and the identity becomes 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = σ²_Yg Var(Y) = 1 Step 6 rescaling only; correlations are scale-invariant Nothing in the mechanism requires the missingness rate to be equal across groups, and nothing requires the two correlations to have the same sign -the (0.5, -0.1) design is verified at step level too.

Discussion

The one thing to do

If the analysis lets groups differ, the imputation model must let them differ in the same way. When the estimand is a between-group difference in association, this means imputing within group -or using an imputation model that gives each group its own conditional slope and its own residual variance. Adding group as a main effect is not a partial fix but no fix at all, because it leaves the entire attenuation in place: what is pooled is the slope, not the means. Adding the group × predictor interaction to one homoscedastic regression is a partial fix and not an equivalent one, which is worth saying because it is the easier thing to do in standard software: it frees the slopes and still pools the residual variance, so the completed variance stays wrong whenever the groups' residual variances differ, and that is one of the two mechanisms this paper reports. At β = (0.8, 1.3), τ² = (0.5, 1.4) and outcome variances 1 and 4, the interaction-only model misses a group's correlation by up to 0.111, while the same model with equal residual variances is exact (verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02. R).

The cost of doing so is small. Across the whole grid, group-wise imputation held bias within [-0.016, +0.021] and coverage within [0.936, 0.974], so it purchased its accuracy at no measurable price in efficiency. In the applied illustration it detected the real species difference as often as listwise deletion did. We therefore see no efficiency argument for pooling in this setting.

The reading rule for a pooled study is asymmetric

Because the failure is one-directional under a statable condition, the reading rule is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the practically useful part.

A study that used default imputation and reported no difference is uninformative about whether one exists. At 40% missing, the procedure removes roughly half the difference on the z scale, and in the applied case it removed all of the detections. That a null report is uninformative holds whatever the groups look like. The attenuation itself, however, is one-directional only within the class we model -standardised groups, a common Y distribution, selection on Y. Outside it the general form permits the completed contrast to be shrunk, exaggerated, reversed or manufactured, which leaves a null report uninformative for a wider set of reasons rather than for this one.

A study that used default imputation and did report a difference cannot be cleared by inspecting its variances.

The "erase only" reading holds only when the null case has a common population conditional slope and residual variance, and comparable-looking marginal sample variances do not establish that: two groups with equal correlations and unequal spread already have unequal slopes, and sampling error puts the required equality beyond the reach of any eyeball check. The defensible rule is procedural rather than diagnostic:

A pooled-imputation result should be re-estimated with group-specific slopes and residual distributions, or under an explicitly congenial joint model, before the reported difference is treated as established. Comparable observed variances are at most a weak warning diagnostic, never a guarantee.

Where the groups' variances visibly differ, the finding warrants reanalysis with group-specific conditional models rather than outright rejection, and a large study reports the artefact as significant more often than a small one does. With equal true correlations and a two-fold difference in the spread of the complete variable, pooled imputation manufactures ζ = -0.121 out of nothing; at a three-fold ratio with 40% missing and N = 640 it declares that difference significant in 31% of analyses ( §Results 4b). The rejection rate rises with N and tends to 1 in those designs, because each has a fixed nonzero contrast limit. Unequal variances alone do not produce one: two groups with no association at all keep a zero contrast exactly, at every rate and at any spread ratio ( §Appendix).

The asymmetry we originally claimed, that pooling can erase but never manufacture, is real in the standardised design and not beyond it. Its engine is that a true null there forces a common X | Y slope and a common residual variance, which is the class pooling leaves untouched, while a real difference forces unequal slopes and is shrunk. Equal correlations with unequal scales breaks the first condition; equal correlations and equal slopes with unequal spread breaks the second; and either breach alone puts the null outside the untouched class and makes the failure run in both directions. We state the condition prominently because the weaker, unconditional version is the more quotable one, and because it is wrong.

That rule differs from the one governing the companion paper's deterministic regression imputation, which can manufacture an effect under much broader conditions. Keeping the two straight matters, because the summary "uncongenial imputation is dangerous" is too coarse to act on. The kind of danger depends on which member of the family the analyst used.

More data makes coverage worse, and the mechanism is standard

The coverage result is neither a paradox nor new asymptotics. It is the standard consequence of an inconsistent estimator combined with a shrinking interval, for which Morris, White and Crowther (2019, p. 2087) give the general statement.

Since the bias is proportional to the estimand and roughly constant in N, while the standard error falls at rate 1/√N, the ratio of the two grows without bound, and the interval becomes both narrower and no better centred. In our grid, coverage at π = 0.40 runs 0.992, 0.974, 0.903 and 0.703 as N goes from 40 to 320, reaching 0.584 on the robustness design.

The practical trap lies in the direction of the error at small N. The pooled arm looks better than nominal when the sample is small, because between-imputation variance inflates its intervals. A researcher piloting at N = 40 therefore sees conservative intervals, concludes that the method is safe, and scales up into precisely the regime where it fails.

The same structure produces the false positives reported in §Results 4b, and the two are best understood as one phenomenon rather than as two findings. Applied to a real difference, that growing ratio destroys coverage; applied to a manufactured one, it destroys Type I control, which rises from 0.026 to 0.309 as N goes from 80 to 640 in the worst cell. Every diagnostic a researcher might use for reassurance, whether more data, tighter intervals, or a significant result, moves in the wrong direction.

Relation to the companion paper

The two papers describe the same mechanism with different consequences. In both, an imputation model omits a term that the analysis model contains, and the estimand attached to that term is attenuated by approximately the missing fraction, with an exact factor κ(π) -not the same κ. At the 40% both papers headline, ours is 0.457 and the companion's 0.384, either side of 0.400. The companion's factor crosses below π near 0.32; ours never does in our range. The companion's omitted term is a product X₁X₂, whereas this paper's is group × Y.

Figure 8 puts both papers' attenuation factors on one pair of axes -ours, and the companion's under both MAR and MCAR, three curves in all -which is legitimate because each κ is the same kind of quantity: the dimensionless fraction of a true effect destroyed. They are not the same curve. Against the companion's MAR factor, ours agrees to 0.010 for π ≤ 0.10 and separates to 0.087 by π = 0.50, with pooling across groups costing more than omitting an interaction at every rate. Both factors are evaluated by quadrature, so the small-π agreement is a feature of the curves, not a limit on the comparison.

The instructive difference lies in the boundary, and it is narrower than the symmetry suggests. Deterministic regression imputation manufactures interactions that are not there, governed in sign by a single selection moment though not in magnitude, and it does so under a wide range of conditions. Pooled imputation is guaranteed not to manufacture a correlation difference whenever the groups match on both the slope and the residual variance, since the closed form then returns exactly zero for any selection on Y; the designs in which we have seen it manufacture one are designs where the groups differ in scale. The two failures are therefore not opposites: one is broadly prone to false positives, the other conditionally so -and its condition concerns population slopes and residual variances, so unequal observed group variances flag the risk rather than measuring it.

Limitations

One selection mechanism. Everything reported here assumes missingness at random on the fully observed variable Y, with a logistic tilt of fixed strength. That assumption is what makes E[X | Y, observed] = ρ_g•Y hold, and hence what makes the closed form clean. It also means that the specific shape of κ(π), in particular the finding that κ/π declines from 1.40 to 1.07 across π, is a property of this mechanism rather than a universal constant of pooled imputation.

Missingness depending on X itself is now partly covered rather than merely disclaimed ( §Results 4a). The exact-zero boundary turns out to be specific to selection on Y: under group-asymmetric MNAR on X, a difference does appear under the null. The practical rule nevertheless survives, because the distortion originates in the mechanism rather than in the imputation, with listwise deletion the most displaced arm and pooled imputation the least. In that setting the pooled arm's Type I error is 0.004, while the congenial group-wise arm reaches 0.073, which is 2.8 Monte Carlo standard errors above nominal. The congenial arm is the anti-conservative one there because of its own displacement rather than because congeniality reproduces a compromised target: group-wise imputation fitted to X-selected cases has a displaced limit of its own, -0.0369 against listwise's -0.0429. None of the three procedures models X-dependent selection, so the experiment does not show that no imputation model could. We have not covered MNAR combined with genuinely different correlations, or missingness driven by an unobserved third variable.

κ depends on the gap, not only on π. κ is not a function of π alone. It rises with |ρ₁ -ρ₂|, from 0.448 at a gap of 0.10 to 0.539 at a gap of 0.90 with π = 0.40, although it is very nearly unaffected by where the two correlations sit, since two pairs sharing a gap at different levels agree to 0.001. That near-invariance is a numerical finding over the levels we evaluated; we have no proof of exact invariance, and the phrase should not be read as one. For the gaps most studies test, meaning 0.4 or less, the variation is under 0.01 and κ(π) may be read as a one-argument function, but the qualification belongs in any statement of the law. That variation is inside the ±0.01 noise floor of a Monte Carlo evaluator, which is how it reads as invariance; at a gap of 0.90 it is eight times that floor. An invariance claim needs an evaluator finer than the effect it is testing.

Normality. Within-group bivariate normality is assumed and used twice. The applied illustration is reassuring rather than decisive, since real sepal measurements are not exactly normal and the incremental prediction survived to 0.010 -its worst discrepancy across the two rates, +0.0061 at π = .20 and -0.0099 at π = .40 -but that is a single dataset.

Result 2 -the completed-data moments

With the pooled model X ~Y + group fitted on the observed cases, So b is a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes, weighted by each group's share of the observed sample times the variance of Y among its observed cases. That is the general statement of which b = (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2 is a corollary: make the groups exchangeable and equally sampled and every weight coincides.

Reduction to the published special case

Set w_g = ½, μ_g = 0, σ_Yg = σ_Xg = 1 and a common selection rule. Then β_g = ρ_g, τ²_g = 1 -ρ²_g, V_o and f are shared, so b = (ρ₁+ρ₂)/2, 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = 1, and the expressions collapse to §Steps 3-5. Checked numerically: the general routine reproduces the special-case value to 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ at π = .20 and 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ at π = .40 (R/drv004_general.R). The general form is verified against simulation step by step on three designs that break every symmetry -unequal shares, means, SDs, correlations and group-specific selection -45 checks, 0 failures (R/verify_drv004_general.R).

The boundary, restated correctly -and necessary in the rate

The null result now follows from the algebra. If all groups share the same slope, β_g ≡ β, then b = β and s² = Σ_g q_g τ²_g ≕ τ², so

The covariance is exactly right. The variance is not, unless τ²_g = τ² as well. So the boundary needs two things, and the special case hid the second by making them the same condition: Sufficient -and necessary, once the missing rate is allowed to vary. Both completed moments are affine in the observed fraction, so matching the groups at every rate is a set of coefficient equations, not the one scalar equation that made cancellation look unavoidable. Solved, they force both conditions: a shared slope alone leaves the variance wrong, a shared residual variance alone the covariance. Cancellation at a single rate survives, and the recorded example does it at 3/5 and nowhere else.

Say what "every rate" buys, because the quantifier carries the whole claim and costs nothing to state. For two groups under missingness completely at random at a fraction common to both, with any positive group shares and any positive outcome variances -equal or not -the completed Fisher-z contrast equals the true contrast at every observed fraction if and only if the groups share the slope, and share the residual variance unless that shared slope is zero. The zero-slope case is the trivial exception: with no association in either group both completed correlations are zero at every rate whatever the residual variances are. Necessity is proved here on the completely-at-random sub-family, which is the stronger reading rather than a weaker one -fewer mechanisms are needed to pin the two conditions down, and sufficiency above still holds for any selection on Y and any number of groups.

The same proof gives something sharper than the contrast statement, and it is the version worth carrying: under either admitted case each group's completed correlation is individually constant in the rate and equal to its true value. The contrast is not preserved by two errors cancelling. So pooled imputation cannot trade one group's distortion against the other's across a range of rates -it can do so at isolated rates, which is exactly what the 3/5 example is, and nothing in a real study tunes the missing rate to a point.

One limitation, and it is about detectability rather than about the algebra. Necessity here is exact equality, and a search over the parameter space finds designs that break both conditions and still preserve the contrast to within 6 × 10⁻⁷ at every rate -a violation no finite sample could resolve. So the boundary separates designs cleanly in the limit and not at all in practice near its edge, and a reanalysis that finds a stable contrast across missing rates has evidence the conditions nearly hold, not proof that they do. The proof itself is symbolic: verify/p36_verify_p2_unequal_variance_necessity_2026-09-16.wls solves the coefficient equations and admits only the two cases above. R/verify_p2_uniform_necessity.R carries the zero-slope exception and the detectability search, and it is numerical evidence that fails to contradict the proof rather than the proof -its own verdict line says so. Both are deposited.

Under the standardised design, ρ₁ = ρ₂ implies β₁ = β₂ and τ²₁ = τ²₂, which is why the boundary looked like a statement about equal correlations. It is not. Equal correlations with unequal scales give unequal slopes, and then pooled imputation manufactures a difference -see §Results 4b, where ρ₁ = ρ₂ = 0.40 and a two-fold difference in σ_Y produces a plim of ζ = -0.121.

The general form matters in the body, not only here

The general form above drops all three of the body's symmetries -equal groups, Y standard normal in both, identical selection. The identity becomes 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = Var(Y | g), the pooled slope becomes a variance-weighted average of the within-group slopes, and the boundary is restated in the form the algebra supportsa shared slope β_g and a shared residual variance τ²_g are together sufficient for a zero contrast to stay zero, for any selection on Y -and, in the rate, necessary.

That correction matters in the body, not only in the appendix: the special case makes those two conditions look like one, which is how we came to state the boundary as a claim about equal correlations. §Results 4b reports what happens when they come apart. The general form is verified against simulation on three designs that break every symmetry -45 checks, 0 failures (R/verify_drv004_general.R).

The closed form is evaluated by quadrature, not by Monte Carlo

The closed form is evaluated by quadrature, not by Monte Carlo. Every moment in the derivation ( §Theory) is a one-dimensional integral of a normal density against a logistic weight; estimating them by simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶ leaves roughly ±0.01 of noise on κ, which is the same size as some of the effects below and would make them undetectable. zeta_plim_exact() in R/drv004_closedform.R integrates them directly and reproduces all four independently verified designs.

κ moves with the gap between the correlations, not with their level κ is nearly invariant to the level, but not to the gap. κ depends on π alone to within 0.010 across three designs, which is inside the noise floor of the Monte Carlo evaluator. Evaluated exactly by quadrature, κ moves with the gap between the two correlations and is nearly invariant to their level: the five designs, and the two sharing a gap of 0.40 at different levels that agree to within 0.001, are tabulated in §Results.

Three things the closed form gives and the simulation does not

Three things follow from having the closed form that the simulation alone would not give: 2. κ can be read off before collecting data, for any π, from quadrature rather than a new simulation -which is what makes the result usable as a planning quantity.

3. It says which feature of the design controls the damage. The attenuation runs through A_g, the observed-case share within each group. We offered that as a prediction rather than a post-hoc account, and §Results 5b has since tested it and rejected it: holding the asymmetric deletion rates almost fixed at 0.267 / 0.532 while equalising the two species' spreads and correlations drops the manufactured displacement from 0.1227 to 0.0001. So the uneven loss of values accounts for essentially none of the applied illustration's excess over the balanced simulation, and the 1.80-fold spread ratio supplies it instead.

The object underneath: attenuation as a moment defect

Restated here, not cited, so this appendix stands on its own. The general treatment is in the third paper of this series (Shavit, 2026b); a reader of this one should not have to hold another manuscript to check the argument.

Everything above computes completed moments and then forms a correlation from them. It is worth recording what governs those moments, because the same three lines govern every estimand of this kind -and because they say precisely where this paper's estimand is different.

The general object.

Write an analysis as a regression of an outcome on a feature vector Z, and let G = E[ZZ′] and c = E[ZY] be its population moments, so the true coefficients are β = G⁻¹c. Under missingness completely at random at rate π, a fraction 1π of rows carry the real features and a fraction π carry features built from an imputed value, so G*(π) = (1π)G + πG_imp, c*(π) = (1π)c + πc_imp, and neither imputed-row moment set depends on π. Both pooled moments are straight lines in the missing rate. The bias is then exactly β*β = G*(π)⁻¹(c*(π) -G*(π)β), and differentiating at π = 0 gives the first-order cost as -G⁻¹d, where is the moment defect of the imputed rows: how far the filled-in rows fall from satisfying the analysis's own normal equations.

The estimator is exact at every missing rate exactly when d = 0. That is normalequation compatibility, not a definition of congeniality in Meng's (1994) sense, which is stronger: preserving the whole imputation/substantive-model relationship forces d = 0, while d = 0 can also arise through cancellation without it. The condition d = 0 is nonetheless sharper than asking the imputation to preserve the joint distribution, which is sufficient for exactness but stronger than necessary.

This paper's estimand is not the easy case.

With the Gram matrix held fixed, a regression coefficient is linear in the cross-moment vector, so the defect converts to a coefficient error in one matrix multiplication -by G*(π)⁻¹ exactly, and by G⁻¹ at first order in the rate. Jointly in both moment sets the coefficient is not linear at all: G⁻¹c is scale-invariant, since multiplying G and c by one constant leaves it unchanged. A correlation admits no such conversion. It is a ratio, σ_XY ⁄ σ_X σ_Y, and the contrast then applies Fisher's transform on top. So the law above does not deliver ζ directly; it delivers the moments, and the ratio and the transform are a further step -which is exactly the step Results 2 through 5 of this appendix take, by hand, for this design.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly. The moments this paper computes are the same objects the general law consumes, which is why the pooled slope b appears in both accounts as the thing the imputed rows are told to believe. And the nonlinearity is not a technicality: because a correlation is a ratio, a defect in the covariance and a defect in the variance can partly cancel, which is precisely why the boundary condition above is necessary only once the missing rate is allowed to vary, and why a single rate can hide a real difference.

Appendix: the mathematics in general form

The special case in the body carries the argument. This appendix drops every symmetry the design assumes -equal groups, a common Y distribution, identical selection -and shows the same law survives. It is verification, and it is also where the boundary condition is stated correctly, because the special case makes two distinct conditions look like one.

No real dataset satisfies those three symmetries, and the applied illustration had to be evaluated by a bespoke routine rather than by the formula. So we give the general result. It is not much harder, it contains the special case, and -as §Results 4b reports -it overturns a claim we made from the special case alone. In words: 𝒜_g is the observed rows' share of group g's outcome variance; ℬ_g is the missing rows' share, together with the shift between the two rows' means. The null is settled exactly rather than estimated. With ρ₁ = ρ₂ we get b = ρ, hence k_g = 0 and Cov_g = ρ(A_g + B_g) = ρ for any selection on Y whatsoever -including selection that differs arbitrarily between the groups. The restriction to selection on Y is not decoration: Step 1 needs it, and §Results 4a shows what happens without it. That exact null is a proof that pooled imputation cannot manufacture a difference in this standardised design, where equal correlations give equal slopes and equal residual variances; a simulation could only ever fail to find one.The same algebra gives more than the null, and the general version is worth stating. k_g = 0 requires a shared conditional slope, and leaving the completed variance alone requires a shared residual variance; neither requirement needs ρ₁ = ρ₂ or equal outcome variances. Suppose β_g ≡ β and τ²_g ≡ τ². Then the pooled imputer recovers exactly those values, b = β and s² = τ², and the completed moments within group g are Cov_g(X, Y) = β•Var(Y | g) and Var_g(X ) = β²•Var(Y | g) + τ² -the group's own population moments, with the missing rate absent from both. So each correlation is preserved exactly, and so is any contrast between them, zero or not, at every rate and under any admitted selection on Y. Unequal outcome variances are permitted and then the preserved contrast is nonzero: at β = 0.8, τ² = 0.5 and Var(Y | g) = 1 against 4, the true ζ = -0.584 comes back unchanged at every rate (closed form and simulation at N = 4 × 10⁶, with controls that fire when either equality is broken: verify/p36_verify_p2_exact_recovery_2026-10-02. R). Within this class pooled imputation does not shrink a real difference either, so the asymmetry of §Discussion is a property of the standardised design -where a null forces the class and a real difference leaves itand not of the class itself.

Groups g = 1, …, G with sampling shares w_g. Within group g, Y ~N(μ_g, σ²_Yg), X = μ_Xg + β_g (Y -μ_g) + ε, ε ~N(0, τ²_g), β_g = ρ_g σ_Xg/σ_Yg (the within-group slope), τ²_g = σ²_Xg(1 -ρ²_g). Missingness may depend on Y in a group-specific way: P(missing | Y = y, g) = w_g(y), an arbitrary function. Write f_g = P(observed | g), and let a_g, V_og be the mean and variance of Y among that group's observed cases, c_g, V_mg the same among its missing cases. The two quantities that carry everything 𝒜_g := f_g•V_og, ℬ_g := (1 -f_g)•[V_mg + f_g•(c_g -a_g)²] the identity, in general 𝒜_g + ℬ_g = Var(Y | g) = σ²_Yg, for any selection on Y, in any group.

Result 1 -

Proof. Decompose Var(Y | g) over the observed/missing split: Var(Y|g) = f_g V_og + (1-f_g)V_mg + f_g(a_g -μ_g)² + (1-f_g)(c_g -μ_g)².
